header.title: Professio Fidei: AI translation (Claude)
header.author: Bachiarius Monachus
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's tmp378.tmp378.opp-lat1, from Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. The whole work is translated. It was chosen because no English translation of it could be found.
header.statement: An AI-generated translation of the whole work, checked against the original by a second AI only in samples. No specialist has reviewed it.
header.availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

Section 1: 'in figuram nostri' follows this text; the scriptural verse is usually read with a plural 'in figura'. 'Pontificis filiis' refers to Aaron's sons. 'Numquid patriarcharum vitam fratrum culpa turpavit' is taken to refer to Joseph's brothers or similar, but the sense is general.
Section 2: 'discipula' applied to Rome is odd and may be corrupt. 'cariosae vel tinnientis lepra haeresis' is obscure; 'tinnientis' (ringing) may be an echo of the tinkling cymbal above, or corrupt (perhaps from 'tinea', moth or worm), and the construction is awkward. 'in centum partes' (into a hundred pieces) is translated as printed. 'commovent' is translated; the edition queries 'commonent' (admonish). The sentence on the middle of the spine is obscure; it seems to mean a region, perhaps Bachiarius's own or the addressee's, where error persists.
Section 3: scanning errors silently read: 'se pullum' as 'sepultum', 'et Fidium' as 'et Filium', 'fide' as 'fidei', 'Bed' as 'Sed', 'unius naturis' as 'unius naturae'. The wordplay on 'altaris' depends on reading 'res alta' from the syllables of the word taken from the end. 'unus Deus, et unus filius de Patre' is translated as printed, though the text may be disturbed here. 'nec est secundus a primo' could also mean 'nor is the second from the first'; '[lower]' is supplied for sense. 'cognitio sua... imago sua' is difficult: taken as men's knowledge and God's image (in us). The double rendering of 'Spiritus sanctus Patris et Filii' but procession only 'a Patre' is as in the text.

Section 4: 'vobis in Adam' is read as 'nobis', and 'qualitatibus e substantiae' as 'qualitatibus et substantia(e)'. Section 5: the opening sentence is awkward, and 'meritura' is read as 'meritum' (desert). The quotation 'Per bonum operatum est mihi...' is given as the text has it; the edition cites Rom. 7:8, but the wording is closer to Rom. 7:13, and it does not obviously support the point. Section 6: 'Virginem novam aliam in secreto' is obscure and may be corrupt; the scriptural allusion is uncertain. 'ne non nisi' is a redundant double negative, rendered as 'only'. Section 7: 'probantes (aliquid) rectius quid dixerint' is garbled, and the rendering is tentative. 'masculinum nostrum' alludes to Exod. 34:23, the appearing of the males. Section 8: 'solum degenere reddit et confessione tinnitum' seems corrupt and is rendered by sense. 'Suracim' is taken as the Shishak of 3 Kings 14:25. The clause 'quia instituti lege huc usque ad finem servare possimus' is unclear, and its object is supplied.

nodes.text: 1. All that has been is the very thing that will be, and there is nothing new under the sun. And again the Apostle: All these things happened as a figure of us. This is proved by the outcome of the present matter, since the sacraments of the Gospel mystery, once enacted, are renewed and celebrated again in the times of our own age. See now, as far as we understand it, Christ asks water of the Samaritan woman, when Your Beatitude requires a statement of faith from us. What makes us suspect, as far as I can see, is not our speech but our region; and we, who do not blush for our faith, are put to shame by our province. But far be it, most blessed one, that among holy men the stain of an earthly birth should taint us. Even if we have known a homeland according to the flesh, yet now we know it no longer, and, desiring to become sons of Abraham, we have left our land and our kindred. We say this because, as with the Samaritans, so we are not believed by the Jews, on the ground that the stain of a certain heresy has touched our native soil. Thus we are judged by the sentence of certain presiding bishops as if we could not be free from the deception of error. In the same way it was once said by unbelievers: Can anything good be from Nazareth? And yet Christ came from there. Did, I ask, the treachery and greed of one man alter the merits of the Apostles, one who came, I will not say from the same region, but from their very side? Did the fault of the brothers disfigure the life of the patriarchs? Did the fabrications of false prophets falsify the oracles of the prophets? When the famous Korah the Levite turned aside into heresy, did the remaining kindred descended from that stock contract a stain from being related to him? When the sons of the high priest offered strange fire, their brothers performed the priestly office, and by the honour of their ministry they bore witness that they were blameless of their brothers' crime. When Nicolaus the deacon turned aside into heresy, the glorious works of the brothers gathered [with him] shone forth in the powers of God. The charge of our region is brought against us. Whoever says this, let him read that Christ [was called] a Samaritan: and in that province they were enslaved to the crimes not only of heresy but of idolatry. In the house of the profane and most wicked Ahab, Obadiah the servant of the Lord was found, who earned a place among the company of the prophets. In Zarephath of Sidon, among the most wicked race of the Canaanites, a faithful widow is found and is chosen as the hostess of the prophets. Balaam, a master of idolatry and a chief of heresy, was permitted to proclaim Christ. Job descended from the profane and faithless stock of Esau. Ruth, a kinswoman of the lineage of Christ, is described as a Moabite woman, whose origin is banished for ever from the doors of the Church. Abraham, the head of faith, descended from the stock of the Chaldeans, to whom the impiety of the magic art is native and natural. When the Magi worship Christ, the old reproaches of their errors are not charged against them. To Moses, trained in the arts of the Egyptians, the grace of the prophetic spirit is granted. Is the error of an earthly province now to be charged to those reborn in Christ?

2. If we acknowledge a homeland, let us blush for its fault too; but for me the city in which I was renewed has become my region and homeland. Let nothing from earthly ties be charged to me, for I remember that I renounced them. Whoever considers me faithless because of my kinship with a province, let him know that he himself is faithless, because he has either forgotten, or thinks unstable, what he knows he confessed in baptism; for without doubt the man who convicts me of my homeland's error does not leave his earthly kindred. Certainly, according to the order of human affairs, a father makes a homeland. How can I be said to have a homeland on earth, when by heavenly command I am not allowed to call anyone father on earth or to have one? Do you want this proved to you by me with clear examples, you who blame me for the error of my homeland? Did not the Novatianists, dissenting from the catholics in this way, contract the leprosy of a shameful heresy through a perverse judgment, because they believed that a past series of faults should be charged to later generations as well, and hated the people rather than the heresy? If for the fault of one man the whole offspring of a province is to be anathematized, let that most blessed disciple too be condemned, that is, Rome, from which by now not one but two or three heresies or even more have sprung up; and yet none of them has been able to hold or to move the chair of Peter, that is, the seat of the Faith. Let all the provinces finally be condemned, from which the rivulets of various errors have flowed. That vessel of election and Teacher of the Gentiles, when Eutychus fell from the third storey (erring, I believe, in something concerning the Trinity), restored to him the warmth of faith and gave him back life, that is, granted him pardon. Us, who perhaps are still sitting at the window, that is, on the way of light and in the splendour of faith, excessively severe judges condemn on suspicion and not after inquiry, not knowing that with the judgment they judge they will be judged, and that whoever says racha to his brother will be liable to the gehenna of fire. For racha is interpreted "empty". And who is empty, except one whose inner parts lack the truth of faith, and who is like sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal? That man who had seen Christ for only a single night said to his fellow tribesmen: Does our law judge a man unless it first hears what he is doing? And do these, who have been followers of the Lord for so many years, judge before they hear and learn the matter on which they judge? If sentence is to be delivered before inquiry, why did the lawgiver command that, before the priest enters and sees the house that is being split by the rotting or ringing leprosy of heresy, it should not be judged unclean? Do not, I beg, most blessed brother, let ill be thought of my province. For it does not escape your perceptiveness that when, at the coming of the Lord's ark, the head of Dagon was shattered into a hundred pieces together with both feet, his spine is described as having remained intact. For we understand the head and feet of Dagon, the limbs of the world, to be the east and the west, in which parts, under the presence of the Law, all the perversity of errors has been crushed. Let it be yours to judge what is the middle of the spine, in which the framework of the joints, though loosened, still persists. Why, I ask, is my province being asked about? I am a stranger, as all my fathers were. If, however, it is pressingly asked where I was born, let my confession be accepted, which I answered in the birth of baptism: for my homeland did not give me a confession, but my confession gave me a homeland; because I believed, and I received. Nor let a Samaritan condition cloud me; for when questioned by Christ at the well I believed, and when cleansed from the leprosy of unbelief I acknowledged [him]. Nevertheless, since the teachings of apostolic instruction move us to give an account of the faith and hope that is in us to all who ask us, let us not delay to show the rule of our faith to Your Beatitude, who are a master builder of this very edifice.

3. But lest perhaps the very fact that I am slow in answering what I was asked should cause suspicion of unbelief: we believe that God is; what he has been, he was; what he was, he will be, never other, always the same: the Father God, the Son God, the Holy Spirit God: one God, and one Son from the Father, the Holy Spirit of the Father and of the Son. This is the substance of the one Trinity, and these three have one will. Neither is the one who imparts greater, nor the one who receives lesser; nor is the second [lower] than the first, nor the third from the second; for so the prophetic teachings have instructed us, saying: You shall not go up by steps to my altar. For we take the altar to be a kind of base of the Faith, from which the nourishment of life-giving food is shared; for the altar, from the proper meaning of its name, is nothing other than the lofty knowledge of sublime things. For the name altaris, divided by syllables and begun from the end, signifies and sounds "a lofty thing". To this Faith we ought not to go up by steps, lest by thinking unequally we make a passage from lower to higher; but we should enter with an equal step of our heart, so that we may understand the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit to be of one substance, of one power, of one might. For the Father is the principal name of divinity in himself, which is believed, and which is said: the Father God, the Son God from the Father, not from himself, but [the Son] of the Father. The Father is God and the Son is God: but the Father is not the same one who is the Son; yet the Father is believed to be the same thing that the Son is. And the Holy Spirit is not the unbegotten Father, but the Spirit of the unbegotten Father. The Son is begotten, not the Spirit a Son, but himself the Son, upon whom the Spirit was sent by the Father. Therefore, since the Father, whose Spirit it is, is unbegotten, it is incautious to call the Holy Spirit unbegotten, lest two unbegotten ones or two Fathers be supposed by the unbelieving. The Son of the Father, begotten by the Father before the ages, cannot have another begotten one as a partner, so that he may be believed only-begotten and two begotten ones may not be spoken of. For the Father is one unbegotten, the Son is one begotten, the Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Father, is coeternal with the Father and the Son; since there is one work and one operation of will in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. The Father is unbegotten, the Son begotten, the Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Father, is coeternal with the Father and the Son; but the one is born, the other proceeds, as is read in the Gospel of blessed John: The Spirit who proceeds from the Father, he will announce all things to you. Therefore let the Holy Spirit be thought neither to be the unbegotten Father nor the begotten Son, but the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Father. But what proceeds is not other than that from which it proceeds. If the person is asked about, he is God. This threefold conjunction and conjoined division thereby both excludes union in the persons and retains unity in the distinction of persons. And so we believe of the most blessed Trinity that it is of one nature, of one deity, of one and the same power and substance; and that between the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit there is no difference, except that the one is the Father, and this one the Son, and that one the Holy Spirit: a Trinity in subsisting persons, a Unity in nature and substance. We believe also that the Son in the last days was born of the Virgin and the Holy Spirit, and took on flesh of human nature and a soul. In that flesh we believe and confess that he both suffered and was buried and rose from the dead; and that in the very same flesh in which he lay in the tomb, he ascended after the resurrection into heaven, whence we await his coming for the judgment of the living and the dead. The Virgin too, of whom we know he was born, [we confess to be] a virgin before giving birth and a virgin after giving birth, lest we be held to be partners in the error of Helvidius. We also confess that the flesh of our resurrection is whole and perfect, [the flesh] of this [body] in which we live in the present age, and are either governed by good practices or subject to evil works, so that in it we may either suffer the torments of punishment for evil deeds or gain the rewards of good things for good deeds. Nor do we say, as certain people most absurdly do, that another [flesh] will rise in place of this one, but this very one, with no limb at all cut off from it nor any part of the body severed. This is the treasure of our Faith, which we keep sealed by the Church's Creed that we received in baptism. So we believe in our heart before God; so we confess with our lips before men, that their knowledge may give men assurance of our faith, and his image may render testimony to God. This is the staff of our defence, with which we may strike the mouths of those who murmur against us, who bark at us as we pass along the road of this world, from the yoke of habit and not from the pursuit of reason. This is the shield of our faith, with which we repel and avoid the poisoned darts of the words of detractors and of suspicions, lest the word of the enemy, aimed to strike, should find in us any exposed limb, bare of the protection of faith. But let us be silent about these things, since we have now undertaken the task not of striking back at the enemy, but only of avoiding him.

4. Now, if we are also asked what we think about the soul, we believe that it was made, as we read in the prophet Jeremiah, where King Zedekiah says: "The Lord lives, who made this soul for us." But if it is asked from what it was made, I confess that I do not know, for I am aware of having read it nowhere. And so I do not blush at my ignorance, because I am not taught it by reading, nor do I fear danger, because I do not presume upon what I do not read, lest I be found a transgressor of the prophetic precepts, which command that blood is not to be eaten, adding that the blood of all flesh is its soul. For what is eating blood, if not disputing about the soul? And so we can say that the flesh which was founded for us in Adam was put together from the qualities and substance of the world, with God as craftsman and author; but the blood let us pour out at the base of the altar, that is, let us leave to him who created it the knowledge of the source from which he created it. For the base of the altar is like a kind of root of the depths, and to its secret let us also join the account of the soul, about which we cannot dispute. And so we do not call the soul a part of God, as some assert, because God is impartible, undivided and impassible, whereas the soul is enslaved to various passions, as the daily outcome of events proves. Nor do we say that it was made from any creature, lest we make it more worthless than the other creatures, over which it has been set as mistress if it acts well; but [we say] that it is formed solely by the will of God, whose power has no need of matter from which to fashion what he wills, but his will itself is the matter of the things he has commanded to come to be or to exist. But neither do we give our hands to that assertion in which some take a needless delight, so as to believe that souls are generated by transfusion; for blessed David contradicts this surmise when he says: "Know that the Lord himself is God: he made us, and not we ourselves." And elsewhere: "Who fashioned their hearts one by one." Where will transfusion find a place here, where either hearts are fashioned one by one, or it is said: "He made us, and not we ourselves"? Those, then, who say that souls are generated by transfusion are said to assert this, that we make ourselves. But prophetic foreknowledge rebukes this by saying: "He made us, and not we ourselves." Apart, therefore, from the Trinity alone, we believe and confess that everything which has power, acts or moves in the heavens, on the earth or in the sea is a creature.

5. We do not hold that the devil was made as the devil now is, nor that he had a kind of nature of his own, so as to be born a devil, and [we hold] that his desert gave him this name, not God; nor that he is unbegotten, because he is not God; nor that he was made a devil, because God did not make evil; but that he was made a good angel, as Scripture shows: "Through the good it worked in me every concupiscence." For I believe that he was an evil angel in the sense in which the Apostle says: "There was given to me a goad of my flesh, an angel of Satan to buffet me." And elsewhere: "Unless the deserter and the falling-away should come." He, then, who is now a deserter was once in the sight of the Creator, and in that sublimity of rank which is described by the prophets, when it is said: "And you were the seal of likeness and a crown of beauty," and the rest; and elsewhere: "How Lucifer, who rose in the morning, has fallen from heaven." We say that he received from his maker a nature capable of good and evil, surrounded with the glory and honour of immortality; that he also received the dignity of knowledge; and that, lifted up in pride, he believed to be his own what was not his, since he did not see as Lord the one who had made him. "I am," he says, "and there is no other besides me." From this he was assigned to earth and ashes, as it is written: "Why are you proud, earth and ashes?" and: "The beginning of sin is pride." Assigned to Tartarus and to everlasting fire, he is [destined] for perpetual punishment, not for immortal life. We believe that every creature of God which has been granted by the Creator for use as food is good, as it was also made: "And God saw that they were very good." But we hold that to abstain from these for a time, not out of religious superstition or abhorrence of God's creature, but for the sake of the flesh's continence, is useful, according to the counsel of the Apostle, who says: "It is good not to eat meat nor to drink wine"; and that to use them when one pleases and to abstain when one is so disposed lies in a person's power. We approve marriages, which have been granted by God's authority; within them we preach continence; virginity, as an outstanding shoot coming forth from the exhausted root of the trunk, we extol and admire. We believe that the difference between the just and sinners arises not from the Creator's making but from the choice of the will. We receive the penance of sinners with the fullest faith, and regard it as a kind of second grace, as the Apostle says to the Corinthians: "I wished to come through you, that you might have a second grace."

6. We receive the Old and New Testaments in an equal balance of faith; and as on a steelyard, whose weight runs along the marks, so we weigh the events of the testimonies with a moving meditation. Without emptying the historical account of credit, we believe that everything we read took place; but according to the Apostle's teaching we search out in these things a spiritual sense, as the Lord may grant, a sense which should nevertheless pertain to the type of Christ and the Church, or contribute to the amendment and correction of morals. And this is in keeping with what the Apostle says: "All these things happened as a figure of us." And elsewhere blessed Peter: "Every saying needs interpretation." Any writing that does not agree or accord with the Church's canon we not only do not receive, but even condemn as foreign to the truth of the Faith. To strange and unknown tales about the contents of the scriptures we do not readily lend assent; nor does a new teaching quickly enter the cavities of our ears, for we read of another new Virgin in secret, who we suppose is an unformed or secret teaching; and she is forbidden to be looked upon for this reason, that she may not deceive the hearts of men with fictions, under the appearance of truth, by the beauty and sweetness of her words. That teaching is a Virgin which is known to no churchman or catholic man; but she has always grown up among women, that is, among souls who, ever learning, join themselves with credulous ease to every spirit of deception, not caring from whom they conceive; although the Lord commanded in the Law that a woman be joined in marriage only from her own tribe, that is, to that understanding of the faith which descends from the seed of the fathers, that is, from their teaching, and is ennobled by the lineage and race of Abraham, who first believed while uncircumcised. That teaching is a Virgin which is pleased with itself only in secret, and blushes to go out in public. Such a teaching we not only flee but also condemn with a public voice, teaching that it is foolish to believe what either we cannot ourselves defend, or ought not to reach public ears.

7. We keep the stricter fasts according to the rule and discipline of the Church, so that three times in the year our male may appear, that is, the work of virtue which excels all other work; and whenever fasts are proclaimed by the Church, we desire then to fast not only from customary use [of food], but also from company, from tales, and from greetings that weave in tales. And although, as God is witness, we hold these things just as we write them, yet we do not so flatter ourselves about the truth that, if perchance priests or teachers, who are the heads of the people and the columns of the churches, on examining anything of what we have professed, should say something more correctly, we would be slow to come over to their opinion; and we remember the written precept: "Ask your fathers, and they will tell you." For we are not so foolish as to be unwilling to humble our hearts to those to whom we bow our heads for sanctification. He is a shepherd: where he calls, I will follow; what he says, I will ruminate on; for he knows that he himself must render an account for keeping me. Let these be the matters on which I could meet you for the present; if there are any things I seem either to have passed over deliberately, or which still trouble you, be pleased to ask without embarrassment, that I may answer without delay, and either be amended of error or be confirmed in the Faith. I testify to everyone who reads the words of this profession that if anyone takes away from these, God will take away his part from the book of life. For as to anyone who believes that we say one thing with our lips and hold another in our heart: as I said above, God can look into our heart. To him we have offered our lips for confession; we have satisfied those matters on which men can judge; and so every word of ours will stand by two witnesses, that is, by God, whose judgement we invoke upon ourselves if we deceive, and by men, whose suspicions we correct by our confession, that they may no longer be willing to sin against us by thinking ill. If anyone, having heard these things, persists in unbelief so as not to give us the assent of faith, I do not doubt that on the day of judgement he will have his portion either among the unbelieving people or among false witnesses, and according to the judgement of the law of Moses he will receive the iniquity which he plots against his brother.

8. For though we are sinners, yet in place of those three hundred golden shields which Solomon fashioned, we ought not to make bronze ones. For the shield is a figure of the Faith, according to the Apostle, who says: "And taking up the shield of faith." And he makes bronze in place of gold who, having taken away the truth of the faith, gives back only a degenerate ringing from his confession; and though he seems devout in the count, he is nevertheless found guilty by his vow, by confessing what he does not believe. Of such, indeed, we should suppose the blessed Apostle to have said: "Having the appearance of piety, and denying its power." Does it not seem to you that power can be perceived in the gold, and appearance in the bronze? But we desire to keep the prophetic assertion, so that before the feet of the king's horses, who are none other than the bishops or teachers, whose feet are swift upon the mountains, bringing good news of peace, we may lay the shields of our faith. For the three hundred golden shields are either faith in the blessed Trinity or the sowing of all creatures, of heaven, earth and sea; and the runners who lay them before the feet of the horses are to be taken as those who were able to say: "I have finished the course"; for, instructed by the law, we may be able to keep [them] even to the end, lest Shishak king of Egypt, that is, the devil, should snatch them away from the temple of our heart. May the support of your prayers keep watch before Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom be glory for ever and ever. Amen.
